Before we begin

Ever since I started following the Acoustical Society of America on social media, I have been bombarded with articles about animal acoustics. As I have said again and again, acoustics is a deeply interdisciplinary field, so its reach into biology is a delightful surprise but hardly unexpected. Animals are our teachers in many ways, and acoustics is no exception. Today, to satisfy your curiosity, let’s look at some fascinating acoustics from the animal kingdom. Another driving force (internal? external?) is my wife, who loves animals. So, on the occasion of her N-th (N = ?) birthday and the approach of Qixi, the Chinese Valentine’s Day, I dedicate this article to her as a birthday present.

“Make sure the sounds of today, don’t become the silence of tomorrow”

Blue whales

Blue whales are masters of long-distance communication. Much of the noise from human activity, however, falls within the frequency range of their calls. Besides interrupting their singing, it also disrupts their rhythm of calling to their friends and getting romantic [1].

To make amends, humans first have to understand how blue whales talk and chat, which means recording them. With humans that is easy; with animals, and especially animals underwater, it is hard. You have to wait for the perfect moment, with no wind and no waves. Dr. Marianne Helene Rasmussen’s team from the University of Iceland spent several months in northern Norway trying to record blue whales. Before you can record them, you have to know where they are, so the team used four hydrophones (think of them as underwater microphones) and beamforming to locate the whales, and then recorded them. Because blue whales communicate with low-frequency sound, the hydrophones were spaced far apart: the team tried spacings of 1 km and 500 m, at a depth of 30 m. In beamforming, the sensor spacing scales with the wavelength of the sound you want to locate, so low frequencies need widely spaced sensors. A 10 Hz sound, for example, has a wavelength of 34 m, assuming a speed of sound of 340 m/s.

The team’s efforts paid off, and the months of work brought a good haul. Here are the sounds of the largest animal on Earth:

Infrasonic calls (we humans can’t hear much of them)

Communication calls

A song when the mood takes them

Golden moles

Golden moles are not born blind. They do have eyes, but the eyes are underdeveloped and covered by thick skin, and with that long, emo-kid fringe on top, the moles might as well be blind. Still, what you lose on the swings you gain on the roundabouts: when God closes a door, he always opens a window. With its unrivaled art of swimming through sand and a pair of golden ears, this mole roams the desert, a hero in its own right. People call it the “sand shark” (in Chinese, a pun on Queen Sea Big Shark, a Beijing indie band).

A specially adapted middle ear, plus a life spent hidden in the sand, lets golden moles use bone conduction to detect seismic waves, which makes them kindred spirits of Zhang Heng, the Han dynasty scholar who built the first seismoscope [2]. A predictive model puts the resonance frequency of their bone-conduction hearing at roughly 100–200 Hz, and the upper limit of their hearing at about 5.9 kHz and 13.7 kHz (for Grant’s golden mole and the Cape golden mole respectively).

Tigers: hearing experts

The tiger’s inner ear is built like a kung fu prodigy’s. It outclasses many of its feline relatives and comes close to humans in frequency resolution. In other words, we and the tigers can hear that the Queen Sea Big Shark mentioned above often sings off-key on stage (for example, singing C-flat where it should be C, which shifts the frequency), whereas animals with poorer resolution can’t tell.

The middle ear collects sound from the outer ear and passes it to the inner ear. There the cochlea, nicknamed “Fourier,” splits the signal into frequency bands with band-pass filtering, converts it into electrical signals and sends them to the brain. I explained the whole process of hearing in detail in an earlier article.

How does the ear tell high notes from low ones?

To sum up the figure below: humans and tigers hear lossless, high-fidelity sound; macaques catch up with humans and tigers at high frequencies; and other animals, such as domestic cats, guinea pigs and chinchillas, hear the compressed MP3 version.

Humans may excel at frequency resolution, but on response time we lose: we are slower than tigers and domestic cats, and even slower than guinea pigs and chinchillas [3].

Congratulations from the chinchilla and the guinea pig

Tigers don’t just hear in lossless quality; they and their close cousin the clouded leopard are also expert responders. Most animals respond faster to high-frequency sounds, but tigers and clouded leopards respond quickly at low frequencies too, even faster than at high ones. Beware the thug with an education: all that muscle plus top-of-the-line equipment, no wonder the tiger became the big boss of the jungle. Scientists suspect that the tiger’s fast response at low frequencies is also directly related to the structure of its cochlea [4].

Animals that learn to talk (vocal learning)

Plenty of animals in nature can imitate sounds. Parrots are the best known, but elephants, bats, dolphins, seals and others are skilled mimics too: at least 164 species of non-primate mammals are capable of vocal learning [5].

A seal called Hoover, for example, could say “Aiya mama!” (roughly “Oh my goodness!”) in a Northeast Chinese accent.

In general, how high or low an animal’s voice is depends on its size: the bigger the animal, the lower the pitch. The koala, however, nature’s noisiest impostor, can imitate much larger animals with a deep, boar-like bellow. It’s a strategy for scaring off enemies, showing off its masculinity and attracting the opposite sex.

(I was pleasantly surprised to discover that WeChat articles can hold more than three videos again. How merciful!)

The monkey bass choir

Fruit flies and hearing aids

Fruit flies keep their sensitive hearing for 50 days of their long, 58-day lives. To put that in perspective: for a human with an average lifespan of 80, it would mean hearing perfectly well until the age of 69, and never once mishearing “Ma Dongmei” as “Ma what-mei?”

This involves some genetics, and the fruit fly’s genetic system is more advanced than ours. Think of it in terms of Windows. As operating systems are updated, older versions are retired: Windows 95, Windows 98 and even Windows XP no longer get updates or support. The life of a fruit fly’s ear works the same way (small as the fruit fly is, it has a full pair of ears!). The genes that are copied later on to maintain the ear’s function are products of continuous iteration, copies of the genes made after the ear has developed. In humans, by contrast, the genes that do this maintenance are still copies of early genes [6]. It’s as if the fruit fly’s system maintenance engineers were young people fluent in Windows 10, while ours were still stuck on Windows 95. As the years go by, their thinking can’t keep up, and our ears give out.

Owls

Owls are famously silent hunters. As the philosopher Zhuangzi once said: “The back of the Peng measures who knows how many thousand li across; the owl, its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky.” A word of warning here: children should read my articles under parental supervision, and where classical Chinese is concerned, the textbook is always right.

The owl’s huge wings are large relative to its body weight, so it doesn’t need to flap often in flight: slow, but very steady. Fewer wingbeats mean less friction with the air, and therefore less vibration and less sound. At the same time, the comb-like edges of the feathers break up the turbulent airflow into small eddies, and the faint aerodynamic noise this produces is further absorbed by velvety down. The result is a forced mute [7].

Comb-like wing edges

Amazing animal ears

To finish, one more curiosity: the weird and wonderful hearing systems of insects. Let’s end this article by learning something new! [8]

Moths

When sound reaches the tympanum, it is picked up by two receptor cells. The first, A1, mainly watches for bats and can detect one 30 m away. Once it senses a bat, the moth changes course, using the weakening of the signal as its cue that it is moving away from the bat and out of danger: it flies in the direction in which the signal fades. The second, A2, is the alarm, the kind you only use at the last moment. When a bat is very close, it sounds the alarm, and the moth breaks into sudden, erratic flight to dodge the bat. The signal goes to the thoracic ganglion and from there straight to the flight muscles, which allows a very fast response.

Mosquitoes

Sound makes the hairs on a mosquito vibrate. The vibration travels down the antenna to Johnston’s organ, where it too is picked up by receptors. Johnston’s organ has about 15,000 receptors, which pick up the vibes of hormones: this is how male mosquitoes go about their naughty business. Get laid, man!

Katydids

Close relatives of crickets and bush crickets. Like moths, katydids sense sound through a tympanum. Better still, they can also pick up sound through their tracheae. And best of all, katydids are rather like mammals: they come with a built-in Fourier spectrum analyzer and can sense broadband sound. They are odd creatures, with their ears on their legs, one on each front leg. The walls have ears? With katydids, it’s the legs.

As in the human inner ear, the sound is passed into a fluid and picked up by cells tuned to different frequencies, which then send the information to the brain.

And that’s not all. Sound picked up through the tracheae travels from the spiracles to the inner surface of the tympanum, and the same process repeats. By comparing the two versions of the sound, the katydid can work out where the source is.
